paras: The turning back of the Elberton colored band from Madison County, Georgia, occurred in August 1885, when a Black band hired by Madison county prohibitionists to play on election day was told on arrival that it would be safer to go home, and left. No violence was reported, and the account survives only as a brief paragraph from the Elberton Gazette reprinted in the Savannah Morning News on 22 August.

According to the Elberton Gazette, the prohibitionists of Madison county employed "the colored band of Elberton" to furnish music there on the day of an election held the week before the Gazette's report. The same Savannah column noted that Madison prohibitionists would wait a year before calling another election, and that prohibition was already established in Elberton.

The band crossed over to Madison county on the day before the election. On their arrival, in the Gazette's words, "they were informed that they would possibly be sater [safer] by returning to this side of the river, which they did without ceremony." The paragraph does not say who gave the warning or why, nor whether the band played on election day. The Gazette added that it did not know "that any violence was threatened them, but they concluded the", and the text breaks off at that point in the surviving copy.
No arrests, official response or later report on the incident appear in the coverage.

The Savannah Morning News carried the item without a headline of its own, among more than two dozen short items in its "Georgia and Florida" column, next to notes on crops, deaths and mail service. The Gazette's wording was light, describing the band's retreat as made "without ceremony," and it disclaimed knowledge of any threat. No other white paper and no Black paper was found reporting the incident.
